name: Stéphane Lambiel
milestone_by_age_26: Won his first World Figure Skating Championship title in 2005 at age 20, becoming the first Swiss man to win Worlds in 48 years, and repeated as World champion in 2006.
early_history_summary: Lambiel began skating at age seven in Saxon, Switzerland, following his sister's footsteps. Around age ten he began training in Geneva under coach Peter Grütter, who recognized his exceptional talent immediately. He won the Swiss novice national championship and spent three years on the junior Grand Prix circuit, winning his first senior national title at age 15 in 2001 and competing at the 2002 Winter Olympics at age 16.
family_context_summary: Born in Martigny and raised in Saxon, Valais, Switzerland. Father Jacques owned a construction/earthmoving company; mother Fernande was originally from Lisbon, Portugal. Parents divorced in 1999. The village created a fan club to help raise funds for his skating costs, which could reach 100,000 Swiss francs per season.
parent_family_domain_summary: No family background in figure skating documented. Father was a construction company owner; mother was Portuguese-born. The family was working-to-middle class in a rural Swiss village.
evidence_summary: Lambiel started skating at age seven and was identified as exceptionally talented by coach Peter Grütter by age nine, who noted he skated with heart and soul. He trained 20 hours per week in Geneva, requiring significant financial support from his family and village fan club after his parents' divorce. His spins and jumping ability were recognized as unusual from a young age, and he progressed rapidly through junior ranks to win his first senior national title at 15 and compete at the Olympics at 16. The combination of a dedicated world-class coach, early specialization, and natural physical talent drove his breakthrough World championship at 20.
starting_point: Born to a construction company owner father and Portuguese-born mother in the rural village of Saxon, Valais, Switzerland; working-to-middle class family.
current_position: Works as a figure skating coach and choreographer based in Lausanne, Switzerland; coaches elite skaters including Deniss Vasiljevs and Kévin Aymoz.

Finished 4th at the Vancouver Winter Olympics in his final competitive appearance.
Retired from competitive skating for the final time on March 9, 2010.

name: Emile Griffith
milestone_by_age_26: Won the world welterweight championship on April 1, 1961 at age 23 by knocking out Benny Paret in the 13th round, and won the New York Golden Gloves championship in 1958 at age 20.
early_history_summary: Griffith grew up in St. Thomas, U.S. Virgin Islands, the oldest of eight children. He moved to New York as a teenager and worked in a hat factory where the owner, a former amateur boxer, noticed his muscular physique and introduced him to trainer Gil Clancy. Griffith won the New York Golden Gloves in 1958 and turned professional the same year, quickly climbing the welterweight ranks to earn a title shot by 1961.
family_context_summary: Born in St. Thomas, U.S. Virgin Islands, the oldest of eight children. Father was a local police constable who deserted the family. Mother Emelda moved to New York to earn money, and Emile followed as a teenager. Working-class immigrant family with no boxing background.
parent_family_domain_summary: No family background in boxing. Father was a police constable who left the family; mother worked in a hat factory in New York. No evidence of athletic or boxing tradition in the family.
evidence_summary: Griffith was discovered by chance when his hat factory boss noticed his V-shaped physique and sent him to Gil Clancy's gym. He had no prior boxing experience but won 51 of 53 amateur bouts and the New York Golden Gloves within months of starting. His natural physical gifts — a 72-inch reach on a 5'7" frame and exceptional athleticism — were immediately apparent. He turned pro in 1958 and won the world welterweight title in April 1961 at age 23, just three years after starting boxing. The combination of raw physical talent and a world-class trainer in Clancy drove his rapid rise despite a late start and impoverished immigrant background.
starting_point: Born in St. Thomas, U.S. Virgin Islands to a police constable father who deserted the family and a mother who worked in a hat factory; oldest of eight children in a working-class immigrant household.
current_position: Died on July 23, 2013 at age 75 in Hempstead, New York; final role was retired boxer who had worked as a corrections officer after boxing.

trajectory.event: Won the New York Golden Gloves 147 lb Open Championship and turned professional, debuting on June 2, 1958.
Won the world welterweight championship by knocking out Benny Paret in the 13th round on April 1.
Regained the welterweight title from Paret on March 24 in a tragic fight that resulted in Paret's death ten days later.
Won the world middleweight championship by defeating Dick Tiger by decision on April 25.
Retired from professional boxing after 112 fights, having won world titles in three weight divisions.
Inducted into the International Boxing Hall of Fame in its inaugural class.

name: Joe Sakic
milestone_by_age_26: Named Canadian Hockey League Player of the Year in 1988 at age 18 after scoring 160 points in the WHL, and made his NHL debut in 1988 at age 19, scoring 102 points in his second NHL season (1989-90) at age 20.
early_history_summary: Sakic grew up in Burnaby, British Columbia, the son of Croatian immigrants. He began playing hockey at age six, inspired by attending a Canucks game at age four. His father built a backyard rink and bought a family membership at the North Shore Winter Club. Sakic scored 156 points in 80 games for Burnaby BC Selects, then joined the WHL's Swift Current Broncos where he was named Rookie of the Year (133 points) and then MVP and CHL Player of the Year (160 points) before being drafted 15th overall by the Quebec Nordiques in 1987.
family_context_summary: Born to Croatian immigrant parents Marijan and Slavica Sakic in Burnaby, BC. Father worked as a commercial fisherman and carpenter/stonemason; mother was a homemaker. Joe spoke only Croatian until kindergarten. Father built a backyard rink and purchased a family membership at the North Shore Winter Club so children could skate. Older sister Rosemarie was a figure skater; younger brother Brian also played in the WHL.
parent_family_domain_summary: No family background in hockey professionally. Father was a Croatian immigrant who loved watching Hockey Night in Canada and actively supported Joe's hockey development by building a backyard rink and buying club memberships. The family was working class but invested heavily in hockey access.
evidence_summary: Sakic benefited from growing up in the Canadian hockey heartland of Burnaby, BC, with a father who built a backyard rink and invested in club access. He was a prodigious scorer from youth hockey (156 points in 80 games in minor hockey) and entered the WHL at 16, where he was immediately dominant. The WHL junior system provided an elite development pipeline, and by 18 he was the top junior player in Canada. His Croatian immigrant background meant he learned English late but absorbed hockey culture completely. The combination of early family investment, the WHL pipeline, and his own intense work ethic and scoring ability drove his rapid rise to the NHL by 19.
starting_point: Born to Croatian immigrant parents in Burnaby, BC; father was a commercial fisherman and carpenter who built a backyard rink and invested in hockey access for his children.
current_position: President of Hockey Operations and General Manager of the Colorado Avalanche; won Stanley Cup as GM in 2022, becoming the first person to win the Cup as both captain and GM of the same franchise.

trajectory.event: Named WHL Most Valuable Player and Canadian Hockey League Player of the Year after scoring 160 points for Swift Current Broncos; drafted 15th overall by Quebec Nordiques.
Made NHL debut on October 6, 1988, scoring 62 points in 70 games as a rookie with the Quebec Nordiques.

Became sole captain of the Quebec Nordiques franchise.
Led the Colorado Avalanche to their first Stanley Cup championship, winning the Conn Smythe Trophy as playoff MVP with 34 points in 22 games.
Won the Hart Trophy as NHL MVP and led the Avalanche to a second Stanley Cup championship.
Retired from the NHL after 20 seasons with 1,641 career points.
Inducted into the Hockey Hall of Fame.

name: Johnny Rep
milestone_by_age_26: Won the European Cup (Champions League) with Ajax in 1972 and 1973, scoring the winning goal in the 1973 final against Juventus at age 21, and reached the FIFA World Cup final with the Netherlands in 1974 at age 22.
early_history_summary: Rep joined local amateur club ZFC Zaandam at age eight and debuted in their first team at sixteen in the Dutch second division. His uncle contacted Ajax, and after a trial he joined Ajax's youth system in 1969. He spent two years in the B-team before breaking into the first team in 1971 under coach Stefan Kovacs, immediately winning the European Cup and Intercontinental Cup in his first season.
family_context_summary: Born in Zaandam, Netherlands, the second son of Cornelis Rep and Aafje de Boer. His grandfather Martinus Rep was a fruit wholesaler in Zaandam. Working-class family with no particular football background; Johnny joined the local club ZFC at age eight.
parent_family_domain_summary: No documented family background in professional football. Grandfather was a fruit wholesaler; father Cornelis (Kees) worked in the family business. No evidence of athletic or football tradition in the family.
evidence_summary: Rep's rapid rise was driven by his proximity to Ajax, the dominant club in European football in the early 1970s. He joined ZFC at eight, debuted in their first team at sixteen, and was scouted by Ajax through his uncle's initiative. At Ajax, he was surrounded by Johan Cruyff, Piet Keizer, and the Total Football system, which amplified his natural pace and finishing. He won the Intercontinental Cup and European Cup in his first season with the first team at age 20-21, scoring crucial goals. The Ajax ecosystem was the primary accelerator, but his natural talent for scoring at decisive moments was essential.
starting_point: Born in Zaandam, Netherlands to a working-class family; grandfather was a fruit wholesaler. Joined local club ZFC at age eight with no particular football background in the family.
current_position: Retired from professional football in 1987; later worked as a youth coach and scout for lower-division Dutch clubs. Currently lives in the Netherlands.

name: Marina Lobatch
milestone_by_age_26: Won the USSR Cup in rhythmic gymnastics in 1985 at age 15, earned a silver medal at the 1985 World Championships at age 15, won World Championship gold in hoop in 1987 at age 17, and won Olympic gold at the 1988 Seoul Olympics at age 18 with a perfect score of 60.000.
early_history_summary: Lobatch started rhythmic gymnastics at age seven in her hometown of Smolevichi, Belarus, when a coach visited her school. She was spotted by Irina Leparskaya, who introduced her to elite coach Galina Krylenko in Minsk. At age ten, Lobatch moved alone to Minsk to join the Republican Olympic Reserve School, commuting from her small town. She rapidly progressed through the Soviet gymnastics pipeline, winning the USSR Cup at 15 and reaching the World Championships the same year.
primary_leverage_engine: Early specialization and Soviet sports pipeline
family_context_summary: Born in Smolevichi, Belarus (then Byelorussian SSR), the third daughter of a carpenter/station worker Vikenty Lobach and his wife Faina, a pastry cook. The family lived in a wooden house and later moved to the first five-story building in Smolevichi. No family background in sports; older sisters did not participate in athletics.
parent_family_domain_summary: No family background in gymnastics or sports. Father was a carpenter; mother was a pastry cook. Working-class family in a small town 120km from Minsk. No evidence of athletic tradition in the family.
evidence_summary: Lobatch's rise was driven by the Soviet rhythmic gymnastics pipeline. A coach visiting her school at age seven introduced her to the sport; by ten she had moved alone to Minsk to train at the Republican Olympic Reserve School under Galina Krylenko, a former world champion. The Soviet system provided elite coaching, facilities, and competitive exposure from a young age. Her natural aptitude — described as having 'good makings for a gymnast' despite being 'merely of angles' — was honed through intensive daily training. By 15 she won the USSR Cup and earned a World Championship silver medal, and by 18 she was Olympic champion with a perfect score.
starting_point: Born in the small town of Smolevichi, Belarus (then Byelorussian SSR) to a carpenter father and pastry cook mother; working-class family with no sports background, 120km from Minsk.
current_position: Works as a rhythmic gymnastics coach and judge for the Belarusian Gymnastics Federation in Minsk; coaches elite gymnasts including Alina Harnasko, a European championship medalist.

trajectory.event: Won the USSR Cup in rhythmic gymnastics for the first time and earned a silver medal at the World Championships in Valladolid, Spain.

name: Goro Shimura
milestone_by_age_26: Created the first theory of reduction mod p of varieties in arbitrary dimensions in 1953 at age 23, which André Weil called 'a very important step forward,' and the Shimura-Taniyama conjecture had its genesis at the 1955 Tokyo-Nikko symposium when Shimura was 25.
early_history_summary: Shimura was born in Hamamatsu, Japan, to a banking family. He survived wartime bombing raids on Tokyo and entered the University of Tokyo in 1949. He graduated in 1952 and was appointed assistant at the University of Tokyo, publishing his first paper that year. In 1953, he created the first theory of reduction mod p of varieties, attracting the attention of André Weil. He was appointed lecturer at the University of Tokyo in 1954 and began his collaboration with Yutaka Taniyama, leading to the Shimura-Taniyama conjecture in 1955.
family_context_summary: Born in Hamamatsu, Japan, to a family belonging to a traditional commercial/banking class from the Osaka-Kyoto region. His father worked for a bank and moved frequently. Shimura was the youngest of five children, with three sisters and a brother. The family had been successful in banking since the late shogunate era, and children in such families typically had private tutors.
parent_family_domain_summary: Family belonged to the traditional commercial banking class (Ryogae) in Osaka-Kyoto, successful for three to four centuries. Children in such families typically had private tutors/nannies. However, no direct evidence of mathematical or academic tradition in the family; Shimura's mathematical interests appear self-directed.
evidence_summary: Shimura came from a traditional Japanese banking family that provided a middle-class upbringing and private tutoring in childhood. His mathematical career was shaped by the University of Tokyo environment, where he studied under Kenkichi Iwasawa and was influenced by Claude Chevalley's 1953 visit. His collaboration with Yutaka Taniyama was the key early multiplier — together they developed the Shimura-Taniyama reciprocity law and the conjecture connecting elliptic curves and modular forms. His 1953 paper on reduction mod p, praised by André Weil, established him as a significant mathematician by age 23. The post-war Japanese mathematical community, though resource-constrained, provided access to international ideas and collaborators.
starting_point: Born in Hamamatsu, Japan to a traditional banking family from the Osaka-Kyoto region; father worked for a bank and the family moved frequently. Youngest of five children in a middle-class household with private tutors.
current_position: Died on May 3, 2019 at age 89 in Princeton, New Jersey; final role was Michael Henry Strater Professor Emeritus of Mathematics at Princeton University.

trajectory.event: Graduated from the University of Tokyo and was appointed assistant; published his first paper on Frobeniusean algebra.
